name: Hualpai

catalog_citation: Watahomigie, Lucille J., Jorigine Bender & Akira Y. Yamamoto. 1982. Hualapai Reference Grammar. Los Angeles: American Indian Studies Center, UCLA. (ERIC ED250132)
catalog_locator: section 2.3 Stress, pp. 39-40 (ERIC pp. 61-62); suffix secondary-stress remark ca. p. 372 (p. 394)
catalog_quote: 2.3 Stress. In the previous sections, we did not explain which part of a word is pronounced louder or higher. When a word contains two or more vowels, we often pronounce one part louder or higher than other parts. To tell us which part is louder or higher (that is, which part of the word is stressed or accented), we can use a stress mark over the vowel--the symbol (´) for the strong and the symbol (`) for the weaker accents. For example, the word for "horse" can be written as òló. This means, then, that we pronounce the word òló with the second o louder or higher. A general rule of the accent placement is as follows: When there are two or more vowels in a word and when one of them is a long vowel, the stress is usually placed on the long vowel. Examples are presented below: vàsú:k 'to be green', jigyó:k 'to bite', wàsí:vk 'to think'. [p.40] A long vowel, then, is usually stressed, there…

new_statements.quote: All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. The canonical shape of a Yuman root may be reconstructed as a monosyllabic morpheme bearing stress (Langdon 1975) [...] Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes. [...] Note that regardless of the complexity of the word, the stress remains fixed on the root. (pp. 239-240) [...] Stress is basically morphological, it is a property of the root (p. 252)

The canonical shape of a Yuman root may be reconstructed as a monosyllabic morpheme bearing stress (Langdon 1975)' and 'Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes'; p. 240 'Note tha…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record is StressTyp2 initial stress, which in this catalog's convention (Czech alternating stress from the left, Polish stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable), Diegueno final stress) means fixed initial stress. Langdon 1977 says stress is morphological, fixed on the root, with a tendency to fall on the LAST syllable of uninflected words; nothing in the article supports initial stress for Walapai or any Yuman language. The Walapai-specific pages (244-245) add no placement statement of their own; the placement claim is the family-wide one, which the article explicitly grounds in the two Walapai descriptions (Redden 1966, Winter 1966).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement covering Walapai (footnote 2, p. 257, lists Redden 1966 'Walapai' and Winter 1966 'Wolf's Son -- A Walapai Text' among the basic sources it rests on): primary stress is assigned morphologically to the root, which is canonically a monosyllable; because Yuman words are built with many prefixes and few syllable-forming derivational suffixes, uninflected words tend to be stressed on the last syllable, but the stress stays on the root however complex the word. For Walapai itself (pp. 244-245) Langdon only discusses the length problem (Redden 1966 vs Winter 1966) and quotes Redden (1966:15): 'A primary-stressed vowel is often higher in pitch than immediately adjacent vowels, but this is by no means always the case. What is heard as stress is a combination of loudness, pitch and length.' She also credits Redden with first noting the stress-timed character of Yuman languages in his work on Walapai.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 240: 'The only thing that can happen to a stressed syllable is that the stress reduces in compound formation to secondary stress on the first member of the compound, thus maintaining the preference for primary stress on the last syllable. Secondary stress in compounds may also further reduce so as to become indistinguishable from other unstressed material.'
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 4, p. 257: 'Some investigators (e.g. Redden 1966 and Halpern 1946-47) describe suffixes which have primary stress so that some "words" in Yuman have two primary stresses. I have ignored these in this paper on the assumption that these forms function as two words.' Mojave (not Walapai) is presented as the one Yuman language with surface stress shifts, derived by retraction rules from underlying root stress (pp. 249-253).
new_statements.identity_note: Langdon uses the name Walapai (spelled 'Walapal' by the scanned); the Walapai-specific discussion (pp. 244-245) rests on Redden 1966 (IJAL 32) and Winter 1966 (a Walapai text, IJAL 32). The article treats Walapai, Havasupai, Yavapai and Paipai together as the Pai group; the stress-placement statement is made for the Yuman family as a whole, not for a particular Hualapai dialect.

tone_statements.citation: Thomas, Kimberly (1990). Vowel Length and Pitch in Yavapai. Proceedings of the 90 Hokan-Penutian Workshop 15. pp. 144-153.
tone_statements.quote: Pitch contours were measured on the same triplets to determine if one or more of these lengths were predictable from pitch. Contours were represented by measuring the onset, midpoints, and offsets from narrow-band spectrograms. Here, ANOVA confirmed that the pitch contours of short, long, and extra-long length categories did not significantly differ from each other. [...] Thus the data show that the three phonetic lengths cannot be predicted from either pitch or syntactic category.

tone_statements.citation: Shaterian, A. V. n.d. [before 1977]. Yavapai Phonology. Unpublished manuscript, cited as 'Shaterian ms' and quoted (ms p. 27) in Langdon 1977: 247-248.
tone_statements.quote: The distinctive pitch accents have a very low functional load. Pitch, stress, and length are interrelated phenomena. Two pitches and three vocalic lengths can cooccur only with primary stress; with secondary stress the two contrasting pitches are neutralized and only two vocalic lengths are present. Furthermore, there is considerable free variation with respect to pitch and length occurring with primary stress; a specific lexical item may carry the same pitch in elicitation form consistently only to appear with the opposite pitch after affixation occurs.

readall_conflicts: The single opened work (Langdon 1977) disagrees with the catalog: the catalog's StressTyp2 record codes Hualpai as fixed: initial syllable (initial stress), whereas Langdon states that in every Yuman language, Walapai included, stress is assigned morphologically to the (canonically monosyllabic) root and that uninflected words therefore tend to carry stress on the last syllable, the opposite edge from the catalog's classification. Langdon does not describe any Walapai-specific deviation from the root pattern; her Walapai section concerns vowel length and the loudness/pitch/length correlates of stress (quoting Redden 1966:15).

audit.recode_to: morphological (set by morphology): one primary stress per word on the root/stem vowel (root usually word-final or followed only by consonantal suffixes/unstressed -a,-i,-o and unstressed auxiliaries; prefixes unstressed). The vowel-length contrast lives on the stressed root vowel and plural/distributive morphology lengthens 'the stressed vowel of the stem', so WBY 1982's 'stress the long vowel' is a reading heuristic (surface corollary), not the mechanism. Edge: not-applicable; weight class: none. The not-fixed/not-initial correction against StressTyp2 (1L) and Gordon 2002 ('Initial') stands unchanged.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: verbatim at the stated pages in held page scan (p.39-40 = PDF 61-62; suffix remark p.372 = PDF 394). (2) Deciding source: a 1982 community/pedagogical reference grammar (primary, linguist co-author, 575 pp, open) whose stress section is a hedged orthographic heuristic; it is not the best available description: a 2001 revised edition exists, and the specialist literature on this languoid (Redden 1966 Walapai phonology; Shaterian 1983/Thomas 1992 Yavapai; Berardo 1992 Hualapai-Havasupai; Langdon 1977 comparative) is unheld. (3) Three open items downloaded now all frame Upland Yuman stress as root stress: Berardo 1992:70 (Hualapai/Havasupai: stressed syllable = morphological root, 'the only part that carries inherent stress'), Thomas 1992:90 (Yavapai: 'Primary stress is always on the root') and 1992:91 quoting Redden 1966:8 (Hualapai: three stress phonemes, vowel length cond
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: quotation verified in source. Held page scan (book p.39 = ERIC p.61) and -p.40 = p.62) carry sec. 2.3 'Stress' verbatim: 'When there are two or more vowels in a word and when one of them is a long vowel, the stress is usually placed on the long vowel' with òló, vàsú:k, jìgyó:k, wàsí:vk (p.39) and 'A long vowel, then, is usually stressed, therefore in this book, the stress mark is not written on the long vowel', Banya:nyuwà, mùlvwayo:wo, thambó ~ thmbó (p.40). Suffix remark 'the suffix receives secondary stress or sometimes weak stress' verbatim on book

sources.quote: 'Words in Yuman languages typically consist of a monosyllabic, stress-bearing root ... Yuman languages regularly stress the final syllable of a word's root, which tends also to be word-final, and so words in Yuman languages typically exhibit word-final stress (Kroeber 1943; Langdon 1977a, 1977b; Wares 1968).' sources.quote: The distinctive pitch accents have a very low functional load. Pitch, stress, and length are interrelated phenomena. Two pitches and three vocalic lengths can cooccur only with primary stress; with secondary stress the two contrasting pitches are neutralized and only two vocalic lengths are present. Furthermore, there is considerable free variation with respect to pitch and length occurring with primary stress; a specific lexical item may carry the same pitch in elicitation form consistently only to appear with the opposite pitch after affixation occurs.

sources.note: Per Langdon 1977:247-248 (held text): for stressed syllables Shaterian sets up 5 vowels, 3 degrees of length and 2 contrastive pitches, gives minimal pairs for pitch (e.g. 'I am sitting' vs 'dwelling, house'; 'be ungrateful' vs 'to scoop out'; 'horn' vs 'tree'), and concedes the pitch accents carry very low functional load, are neutralized under secondary stress and vary freely / flip after affixation; Langdon adds that all pitch pairs involve short root-final vowels (pitch preserving an old length contrast).

sources.note: The practical orthography writes five vowels short vs long (a/aa etc.) and an acute accent for the stressed vowel ('more stress and loudness'); reduplicated words carry an accent on each copy; epenthetic schwa described; there is NO marking or mention of pitch or tone - i.e. the current community standard for Yavapai treats prosody as stress + two lengths only (contrast Shaterian 1983's three lengths and two pitch accents).

tone.quote: Every Yavapai word has at least one accented vowel (á,é,í,ó,ú). Accented vowels are pronounced with more stress and loudness than the other vowels in a word. If the accents falls on a long vowel, only the first of the two has the accent mark (áa, ée, íi, óo, úu).

tone.quote: Pitch contours were measured on the same triplets to determine if one or more of these lengths were predictable from pitch. Contours were represented by measuring the onset, midpoints, and offsets from narrow-band spectrograms. Here, ANOVA confirmed that the pitch contours of short, long, and extra-long length categories did not significantly differ from each other. [...] Thus the data show that the three phonetic lengths cannot be predicted from either pitch or syntactic category.
tone.locator: abstract, JASA 88(S1) p. S53 (Crossref record abstract field)
tone.says: Acoustic test of Shaterian's three vowel lengths in Yavapai (c. 10 tokens per category): durations differ by 100-150 ms and ANOVA supports three phonetic lengths; pitch contours (onset, midpoint, offset) of short, long and extra-long categories do NOT differ significantly, so length is not predictable from pitch (nor from syntactic category); contrastive pitch as such is not tested.
